composition: Nominal composition (wt.%, Table 1): C 0.028, N 0.0034, Ni 15.05, Cr 11.06, Mn 1.09, Si 0.002, Al 0.05. This is the unalloyed reference of the series: Si and Al are at residual/specification levels (Si 0.002 wt.%, Al 0.05 wt.%) whereas the sibling alloys deliberately add ~2.5 wt.% of one of these elements. The base element is Fe (balance not explicitly printed in the table). Ni (~15 wt.%) and Cr (~11 wt.%) are the austenite stabilizers that retain the FCC austenite to room temperature; the composition is otherwise nearly identical to the 2.5 Si and 2.5 Al alloys, which is what allows differences in lattice parameter and SFE to be attributed solely to the Si and Al content differences.
conclusions: In the Fe–Ni–Cr system studied, 2.5 wt.% Al alloying increases the austenite lattice parameter by 1.41 × 10⁻³ nm relative to the base alloy, while 2.5 wt.% Si has little effect. The base alloy is fully austenitic and coarse-grained, and its SFE (26.3 ± 3.0 mJ m⁻²; text 26.3 mJ m⁻²) is consistent with literature values for similar 15 Ni–11 Cr alloys. Compared with this base value, 2.5 wt.% Al raises the SFE by 12–17 mJ m⁻² and 2.5 wt.% Si lowers it by 6–7 mJ m⁻², giving empirical linear coefficients A_SFE(Si) = −2.6 mJ m⁻² wt.%-1 and A_SFE(Al) = 4.9 mJ m⁻² wt.%-1 that agree with high-Mn steel literature and thermochemical modelling. The base alloy also serves as the anchor for showing that Al must be accounted for when extracting austenite carbon content from lattice-parameter measurements, since neglecting Al can overestimate C by ~0.15 wt.%, a non-negligible error for AHSS austenite stability assessments (consistent with the strain-field-corrected upper estimate that would raise A_Al^SFE to ~6.9 mJ m⁻² wt.%-1).
mechanisms: Austenite retention: the base alloy is fully austenitic at room temperature because Ni (15.05 wt.%) and Cr (11.06 wt.%) alloying thermodynamically stabilizes the FCC austenite, rather than retention by carbon partitioning as in AHSS; this single-phase, coarse-grained (~140 μm) microstructure enables XRD analysis without element-partitioning assumptions and makes TEM dislocation analysis of the SFE feasible.

Dislocation dissociation: perfect dislocations gliding in {111} planes lower their elastic self-energy by dissociating into two Shockley partial dislocations bounding an intrinsic stacking fault, with an equilibrium separation d set by the balance between the elastic repulsion of the partials and the stacking fault energy — small SFE gives large separation and vice versa.

SFE from measured dissociation width: the paired (d, α) data obey Eq. (1), SFE = G|a0|²(2−ν)/[48π(1−ν)]·(1/d)·[1 − (2ν·cos2α)/(2−ν)], where d is the partial separation and α the perfect-dislocation character angle; the base alloy gives SFE = 26.3 ± 3.0 mJ m⁻², and in the base alloy the measured separation increases with dislocation angle.

Elastic-constant sensitivity: replacing the isotropic constants used in the final calculation (G = 74 GPa, ν = 0.3) with effective anisotropic values for a 12 Ni–12 Cr steel (G = 66 GPa, ν = 0.43) raised the calculated SFE of the 2.5 Al alloy by ~10% but had little effect on the base (and 2.5 Si) alloy, so isotropic properties were adopted.

Cross-validation of the method: the base alloy SFE of 26.3 mJ m⁻² agrees with the ~30 mJ m⁻² obtained for a similar 15 Ni–11 Cr alloy by TEM analysis of extended dislocation nodes, supporting the dissociation-based SFE determination used here.

SFE–austenite stability link: a low SFE promotes planar shear-band (including ε-martensite) formation whose intersections can act as α′ martensite nuclei, so raising SFE suppresses shear banding and strain-induced martensite; the base SFE therefore sets the reference level for judging how Al (raises SFE) and Si (lowers SFE) modify austenite stability.

Lattice-parameter/C-content interaction: because Al expands the austenite lattice (A_Al^LP = 0.582 × 10⁻³ nm wt.%-1 determined from the base-vs-2.5Al comparison), ignoring Al in XRD-based carbon estimation overestimates the austenite C content by δ_C = x_Al(A_Al^LP/A_C^LP), i.e. 0.125–0.176 wt.% for 1 wt.% Al, whereas Si has a negligible lattice-parameter effect (base and 2.5 Si points coincide in Figure 2).
microstructure: As-annealed structure is fully austenitic and single-phase with a coarse grain size of approximately 140 μm. The austenite is FCC and is retained to room temperature by Ni and Cr alloying, not by carbon partitioning (as would be the case in commercial AHSS). No precipitates are reported. The steel is single phase, so there are no interphase boundaries; the relevant planar defect "interfaces" are stacking faults between dissociated partial dislocations. The introduced deformation substructure consists of dislocations that are dissociated into Shockley partial dislocations bounding stacking faults in {111} planes; grains with a near-{111} orientation (favourable slip during compression) were selected for analysis, and the evaluated dissociated dislocations were confirmed by g·b_p analysis to lie in the {111} plane approximately normal to the electron beam.
processing: Processing route (shared with the other two steels of the study): (1) vacuum casting/solidification; (2) homogenization for 20 h at 1200 °C; (3) hot rolling; (4) solution annealing for 1 h at 1040 °C (the temperature listed for the base alloy in Table 1), chosen to produce coarse grains of approximately 140 μm. This final anneal is the step that defines process_id proc_anneal-1040c-1h. For the TEM/SFE work, additional specimen preparation was applied: 12.7 mm diameter cylinders were machined with their axes parallel to the rolling direction and uniaxially compressed to 5% true strain to introduce dislocations; thin slices were then sectioned at 45° from the compression axis and prepared for TEM by grinding and electropolishing in 95% acetic acid + 5% perchloric acid.
properties: No mechanical properties (strength, elongation, hardness) or physical/servicing property data are reported for this sample. The quantitative performance-relevant quantity is the stacking fault energy: SFE = 26.3 ± 3.0 mJ m⁻² (Figure 3 legend; text gives 26.3 mJ m⁻²), which is consistent with the ~30 mJ m⁻² reported for a similar 15 Ni–11 Cr alloy from TEM analysis of extended dislocation nodes. Partial dislocation separation measured in the base alloy increases with dislocation character angle. The austenite lattice parameter a0 of the base alloy is not given as an explicit number in the text; in Figure 2 the base datum (at relative alloying = 0) lies just above the 0.358 nm gridline and clearly below 0.359 nm (with a small vertical error bar). Characterization techniques applied to this sample: X-ray diffraction (Phillips X'Pert diffractometer, Cu Kα, λ = 0.154060 nm; HighScore Plus 3.0.5 software; specimens ground to 600 grit and chemically polished 20 min in 10 water : 10 H₂O₂ : 1 HF, with a0 from cos²θ/sinθ linear-regression extrapolation to θ = 90°, weighted toward higher-angle peaks, averaged over five of seven coupons after discarding the highest and lowest), and weak-beam dark-field TEM (Phillips CM12 at 120 kV, g3g conditions with (220)-type reflections, s_g ≈ 0.22 nm⁻¹) for dissociated-dislocation imaging and SFE determination.
summary: The "Base" alloy is the reference (unalloyed, i.e. no deliberate Si or Al addition) member of a set of three vacuum-cast austenitic Fe–Ni–Cr steels used to isolate the effects of Si and Al on the austenite lattice parameter and stacking fault energy (SFE). It was vacuum cast, homogenized 20 h at 1200 °C, hot rolled and solution annealed 1 h at 1040 °C to give a fully austenitic, single-phase coarse-grained microstructure (~140 μm). Its role in the study is to anchor the composition comparisons: relative Si/Al alloying is defined against the base, and the base SFE (26.3 ± 3.0 mJ m⁻²) measured by WBDF TEM of dissociated dislocations is the baseline against which the 2.5 Si and 2.5 Al alloys are compared.
unmapped: SFE of the base alloy = 26.3 ± 3.0 mJ m⁻² was read from the Figure 3 legend / text; the base alloy does not display a numeric lattice parameter a0 in the paper (only a plotted point just above 0.358 nm at relative alloying = 0).

Study-level empirical coefficients derived from the three-alloy comparison (Table 2): A^LP(Si) = −0.018 × 10⁻³ nm wt.%-1 [−0.009 at.%-1], A^LP(Al) = 0.582 × 10⁻³ nm wt.%-1 [0.289], A^SFE(Si) = −2.6 mJ m⁻² wt.%-1 [−1.3], A^SFE(Al) = 4.9 mJ m⁻² wt.%-1 [2.5]; the Dyson and Holmes reference values are ≈0 for Si and 0.56 [0.28] for Al for A^LP. These are alloy-system-level results, with the base sample contributing the reference datum.

Methodological caveat: isotropic elastic constants (G = 74 GPa, ν = 0.3) were used in the final SFE calculation because elastic anisotropy was not evaluated and literature effective ν is closer to 0.3 than 0.43; the Williams and Carter partial-dislocation strain-field correction was not applied to the measured separations because not all TEM parameters were available (an upper-limit estimate would raise the 2.5 Al SFE to 44.0 ± 9.8 mJ m⁻² but change the base alloy by ~1 mJ m⁻² or less).

Applicability note: the experimental alloys are fully austenitic and coarse-grained by design, so the SFE analysis assumes a single-phase structure; extending the results to multiphase low-alloy AHSS assumes that the effects of Si and Al on austenite characteristics are independent of Ni and Cr alloying.
